title: Chicken thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is dark‑meat from the upper leg of a chicken, known for its rich flavor and higher fat content than breast meat. When fried in a coating, a crispy crust forms, but in this product the skin and coating are not consumed and serve only as a cooking medium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more iron and zinc than breast meat.
Frying in a coating raises the calorie count by roughly 30 % compared with plain meat.
In many cuisines, thighs are traditionally breaded with flour, egg, and spices before frying.
A properly fried crust locks in juices, keeping the meat moist.
Chicken is one of the most affordable high‑quality protein sources worldwide.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B6, niacin, and riboflavin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Iron, zinc, and phosphorus in the meat contribute to blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium and vitamin B6 help maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: The fat in thigh meat offers sustained satiety and a steady energy source.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Frying adds saturated fats, so people with cardiovascular concerns should limit intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may react to chicken proteins.

items.title: Cooking contaminants
items.content: Overheating oil can produce harmful compounds such as acrylamide; fry at moderate temperatures.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fried thigh hot, cutting it into bite‑size pieces. Remove the skin and coating before eating if desired. Pair with vegetables, potatoes, or a fresh salad. Light sauces—yogurt‑based, tomato, or herb—enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw thighs refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked pieces store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. Freeze at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Discard if an off‑smell or slimy texture develops.
